title: The tree on the road (Avot 3:7)
hook: a hard saying warns against breaking off study to admire a tree; many teachers read it as: the tree is Torah too
tomorrow: how bad is it to forget what you learned?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elazar of Bartota's open hand: you and yours are his, so giving is giving back. The same mishnah keeps going, out onto a road, and says something odd.

Mid-run, a sky goes pink and orange, and somebody stops dead on the path to take a photo. Harmless, surely. So why would a sage frown at someone admiring a tree? Avot has the line, and it's one of the hardest in the book. Rabbi Yaakov says: one who walks on the road reviewing his learning, and breaks off to say, how beautiful is this tree, how beautiful is this field, Scripture counts it as if he put his life at risk. A tradition against trees?
screen: `STOPPED DEAD FOR A SUNSET.` → `HOW BEAUTIFUL IS THIS TREE.` → `A TRADITION AGAINST TREES?`

segments.voice: That can't be it, and the proof is in the Talmud. It gives a blessing for anyone who goes out in the spring month of Nisan and sees trees in blossom, thanking God, who left nothing lacking in His world and made good trees for people to enjoy. Deuteronomy, protecting fruit trees even in a siege, says, "for the tree of the field is man's life." A tradition with a blessing for blossoms isn't telling anyone to ignore them. So what's wrong on that road? Look at one word: he breaks off. He stops studying in order to admire, as if the tree were out there and the Torah in here, and he has to choose. Some teachers read the warning exactly there: the mistake is splitting the world in two. The tree is Torah too, if you look at it as part of the learning. Say the blessing, and admiring becomes study. Other readers hear it more plainly, as a warning about distraction on a dangerous road. Both readings keep the walker's attention whole. The puzzle's answer, on the first reading, is lovely: the sage isn't frowning at the tree. He's frowning at the line drawn between the tree and God.
screen: `A BLESSING FOR BLOSSOMS.` · `THE TREE OF THE FIELD IS MAN'S LIFE.` · `THE PROBLEM IS BREAKING OFF.` · `NO LINE BETWEEN TREE AND GOD.` · then, large: `THE TREE IS TORAH TOO.`

segments.voice: Find one living thing you can see from here: a tree out the window, a houseplant, a weed in a crack. Look at it the way you'd read a line, slowly, finding one detail you missed, a vein, a color, a bent stem. Some Jews say a blessing on seeing a beautiful tree; if you pray, you can let that thanks rise now.
The tree on the road: Avot's hard saying about breaking off study to admire a tree, read by some teachers as a warning against splitting the world from the holy.
screen: `THE TREE ON THE ROAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the tree is torah too. Look at it that way and the walk becomes study. See you on the road.

notes: Attribution: the tree saying is Rabbi Yaakov's in common printed editions; some name Rabbi Shimon. Its number is 3:7 or 3:9 depending on edition. Confirm.
'The tree is Torah too' (the index's 'many teachers') is hedged as 'some teachers'; the second, plainer reading (distraction on a dangerous road) is offered alongside. Confirm both are fair readings.
Berakhot 43b blessing paraphrased: 'who left nothing lacking in His world and created in it good creatures and good trees for people to enjoy.' Confirm.
Deuteronomy 20:19 KJV phrase quoted; the Hebrew is read differently by some (as a question). Confirm.
